title: GitHub Actions from zero
bridge: A workflow file is like a Playwright config plus a test file. It says when to run and which steps to run, on a machine GitHub or we provide. Except: every job starts on a fresh machine. Nothing from your laptop or from another job is there unless a step puts it there.
intro: Every check on a PR, every image build and every agent trigger in this platform is a GitHub Actions workflow. This lesson teaches you to read one and write one. You will use a scratch repo of your own, so nothing touches fcp.

picture.caption: A push arrives and GitHub matches it against the triggers. A job runs on a fresh runner, and the result shows on the PR.

steps.text: pushes a branch and opens a PR (an event)
reads every workflow file and matches the event against its on: block
starts one fresh machine per job, with the runs-on label
runs the steps in order; a failing step stops the job
shows green or red on the PR

sections.h: Start from a file you already run
p: Open fcp/.github/workflows/frontend-ci.yaml. Every time you push a frontend branch, this file decides what runs. It is YAML: indented keys and values, like a JSON object written without braces.
Below is the top of that file, shortened. We will name each part of it in the next sections, so read it once now and come back to it.
sections.because: We start from the real file because every platform workflow has the same four parts. They are a name, an on: block, permissions and jobs.

code.text:
name: "[FRONTEND] - CI"
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    types: [opened, reopened, synchronize]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  check-changes:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/_check-changes-reusable.yml
    with:
      pattern: '^frontend/|^common/workflows/'
      component: frontend

  unit-tests:
    name: Unit Tests
    runs-on: fcp-runner-set
    needs: check-changes
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || needs.check-changes.outputs.has_changes == 'true'

notes.text: The name GitHub shows in the Actions tab and in other workflows that wait for this one.
on: lists the events that start this workflow. Here: a push to main, a PR against main, or a button click.
types narrows the pull_request event. Without it, GitHub also runs on labels, assignments and more.
workflow_dispatch adds a Run workflow button and a gh command. No value is needed after the colon.
permissions says what the job's own GitHub token may do. Everything not listed is off.
jobs is a map. Each key (check-changes, unit-tests) is one job, and each job gets its own machine.
uses: with a path calls another workflow file instead of listing steps. Lesson p2-2 explains this.
name is what the PR shows as the check's name. The ruleset in p2-4 refers to this exact text.
runs-on picks the machine by label. fcp-runner-set is our own runner pool on the inf cluster.
needs makes this job wait for check-changes. Without needs, jobs run at the same time.
if: skips the job unless the branch is main or frontend files changed. A skipped job counts as passing.

p: An event is something that happens in the repo: a push, a PR opened, a comment, a timer, another workflow finishing. The on: block lists the events this file cares about. GitHub keeps the event's data (the branch, the PR number, the commit message) and hands it to the run as github.event.

The most common are push (code arrived on a branch) and pull_request (a PR was opened or updated). workflow_dispatch means someone clicked Run. Two more: schedule (a cron timer, in UTC) and workflow_run (another named workflow finished).

Two fcp facts to remember. cloud-ci.yml, client-ci.yml and sdk-ci.yml run on push to any branch; frontend-ci.yaml runs on pull_request. And a workflow_run workflow only runs from the copy of the file on the default branch, main. You cannot test it from a branch; you merge it, then test it with a throwaway branch.

callout.text: schedule uses cron in UTC with five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, weekday. '17 3 * * 6' in weekly-dependency-upgrades.yml means 03:17 UTC every Saturday. Jobs with schedule only run from main.

p: A job is a list of steps that run on one machine. The machine is called a runner. GitHub starts a fresh runner for every job, runs the steps, and throws the runner away. Two jobs never share a disk, so a file built in job A does not exist in job B.

runs-on picks the runner by a label. fcp uses fcp-runner-set: our own pool of single-use pods in the inf-rhinohealth Kubernetes cluster. A pod is a running container; lesson p5-1 teaches pods and clusters. A tool called ARC (Actions Runner Controller) starts a fresh pod for each job.

Byte uses byte-runner-set, the infrastructure repo uses infrastructure-runner-set. GitHub-hosted labels such as ubuntu-22.04-2core are also allowed in fcp. The allowed labels are listed in fcp/.github/actionlint.yaml.

Jobs run in parallel unless one names another in needs. A job can expose outputs, and a later job reads them as needs.<job>.outputs.<name>. That is how unit-tests above asks check-changes whether frontend files changed.

callout.text: Why our own runners? They sit inside inf, our internal cluster, so they can reach internal services. A GitHub-hosted machine cannot reach them. Two examples: the trigger service in G5-12, and the inf ECR registry (AWS's store for Docker images).

p: A step is one thing the runner does. There are two kinds. A run step runs shell commands. A uses step runs an action: a packaged step someone published, named owner/repo@version, such as actions/checkout or actions/setup-node.

Steps share the same machine and the same working directory, so a file written by step 2 is there for step 3. To pass a value between steps, write name=value to the file named in $GITHUB_OUTPUT and give the step an id. Later steps read it as steps.<id>.outputs.<name>.
The workflow below is the one you will push to your scratch repo in the lab. It is small on purpose.
sections.because: We write the smallest complete workflow first, because every bigger one is this file with more steps and more jobs.

code.text:
name: Hello
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  hello:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Check out the code
        uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - name: Count files
        id: count
        run: echo "files=$(git ls-files | wc -l | tr -d ' ')" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - name: Say hello
        run: echo "Hello from $RUNNER_OS, ${{ steps.count.outputs.files }} files"

notes.text: Give the token the least it needs. contents: read lets checkout clone the repo and nothing more.
ubuntu-latest is a GitHub-hosted runner, free for a public repo. fcp would say fcp-runner-set here.
The runner starts empty. This action clones your repo into the working directory. The long hash is the exact version; p2-2 explains why.
id lets other steps refer to this step's outputs.
Writing name=value to the $GITHUB_OUTPUT file is how a step publishes a value.
${{ }} is an expression. GitHub replaces it with the value before the shell runs. $RUNNER_OS is a plain environment variable GitHub sets.

sections.h: Permissions: what the job's token may do
p: Every job gets a short-lived GitHub token called GITHUB_TOKEN. It can act on this repo only, and only in the ways permissions allows. If you leave permissions out, the repo's default applies, which can be read and write on everything.

Write the block at the top of every workflow, with the smallest set. contents: read for a clone. pull-requests: write to comment. id-token: write only when the job must prove its identity to AWS or Vault (lesson p2-3). The GitHub App in p2-4 is a different, stronger identity; GITHUB_TOKEN is the job's own.
A called workflow cannot ask for more than its caller gives. The comment in fcp's byte-review.yml says it in one line: leaving out issues: read made every run fail at startup.

callout.text: GITHUB_TOKEN cannot push a change that touches .github/workflows, and our agents' App has no workflows permission either. A workflow cannot rewrite the checks it is judged by.

sections.h: Reading a run from the terminal
p: You do not need the browser. gh run list shows the latest runs, gh run watch follows one, and gh run view --log prints every step's output. Each line of the log carries the job and step name, so you can grep it.
When a run is red, read the first failing step, not the last line. Later steps often fail only because an earlier one did.
sections.because: We read runs from the terminal because the agents and the metrics job read them from the API the same way. A run has jobs, a job has steps, each with a conclusion.

code.text:
gh run list --workflow hello.yml --limit 3
RUN_ID=$(gh run list --workflow hello.yml --limit 1 --json databaseId --jq '.[0].databaseId')
gh run view --log "$RUN_ID"

notes.text: Lists runs of one workflow file: status, title, branch, event, id and duration.
Gets the newest run id as JSON. --jq picks the field, the same way the metrics job will.
--log prints the full log. Add --job <id> to see one job only.

lab.faded: Add a second job named report that has needs: hello and prints the files output of the first job. You need to add an outputs: block under the hello job (outputs: files: ${{ steps.count.outputs.files }}) and read it as needs.hello.outputs.files. The last line of the report step is left for you.
lab.alone: Add a schedule trigger that runs every day at 02:20 UTC. Add a third job named fail that runs the command exit 1. Push it, run it with gh workflow run, and read the log of the red run. Find which step failed and which steps never ran.
lab.done: gh run list shows a green run with two jobs, and a red run where fail failed and report still passed.

quiz.q: A file is written by step 2 of job A. Where can step 1 of job B read it?

options.text: Nowhere: job B runs on a different fresh machine.
options.why: Each job gets its own runner. To share files you upload an artifact (a file GitHub keeps for the run), or pass small values through outputs.

options.text: In the same working directory, because both jobs check out the same repo.
options.why: Checkout gives job B a fresh clone of the commit, not job A's working tree.

options.text: Through needs: the file is copied over automatically.
options.why: needs only orders the jobs and passes outputs (strings), never files.

quiz.q: You add a new workflow with on: workflow_run on a branch and open a PR. It never runs. Why?

options.why: Permissions change what the token may do, not whether the workflow starts.

options.text: workflow_run workflows only run from the copy of the file on the default branch.
options.why: GitHub reads workflow_run and schedule triggers from main. Merge first, then test with a throwaway branch (G5-12 says exactly this).

options.text: The branch name must start with the workflow name.
options.why: Branch names never gate a workflow unless the on: block filters them.

quiz.q: A required check (a check the PR must pass before it can merge, p2-4) is named after a job. That job has if: false on this PR. What does the PR show?

options.text: A pending check that never finishes, so the PR cannot merge.
options.why: That happens when the whole workflow does not run because of a paths: filter. A paths: filter is an on: rule that starts the workflow only when certain files change. That is why G0-02 removes those filters.

options.text: A skipped job, which counts as passing.
options.why: A job skipped by if: reports 'skipped', and rulesets treat it as success. G0-02 relies on this through check-changes.

options.text: A failed check, because the job produced no result.
options.why: Skipped is its own conclusion, separate from failure.

words.plain: One YAML file under .github/workflows that says when to run and what to run.
Something that happens in the repo (push, pull_request, schedule) and can start a workflow.
A list of steps that run on one fresh machine; jobs run in parallel unless needs orders them.
The machine a job runs on, picked by the runs-on label; fcp-runner-set is our own pool on inf.
One command (run) or one packaged action (uses) inside a job.
A published, reusable step named owner/repo@version, such as actions/checkout.
The short-lived token every job gets for this repo, limited by the permissions block.

tickets.why: Renaming the 'Unit Tests' jobs and removing paths: filters needs you to know what a job name and an on: filter do.
The routine trigger is a workflow_run workflow on fcp-runner-set with a job-level if: on the branch name.
The workflow-lint file is a push workflow with paths and the least permissions, copied into every repo.
BYTE-GOLD is a pull_request plus push plus schedule workflow with a concurrency group (one run at a time per group).

remember: A workflow is events in, fresh machines per job, steps in order, and a token that can do only what permissions says.
